column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check

SKIPPED: article under 250 words of substance; its penalties and the 797 capitulary are already in the description The article gives 782 traditionally, occasionally 785, and says 795 is also considered possible; the entry dates it c. 782-785.
The article titles him Caradog ap Gruffudd; the entry spells Gruffydd. Both forms of the name are left to the entry.
The article does not tell his death beyond the date, so there is no Death and legacy section.

The entry says he was sent in 1810 as a royal commissioner of the Regency; the article says he was appointed in Cádiz by the Supreme Central Board. The text names neither body. The article's account of rumours about his relationship with Humboldt is left out.
The article says the bishopric was established around 350 but also that its bishops attended the Council of Elvira in the first half of the 4th century; the text gives only the fourth century.

The article also cites another source by which six brigades went to the Black Sea Host; left out, as the entry speaks of its western regiments. The article's paragraph on 1786 and on four civilian villages assigned 'as early as 1832' is muddled and was left out.
Short article, much of it a quotation; text kept to about 270 words.

The article's opening lists the towns as Brussels, Antwerp, 's-Hertogenbosch, Tienen and Zoutleeuw, omitting Leuven, which its translation of the charter gives three seats; the text gives the council's seats from the translation and does not count the signatory towns. The entry's account of the dying duke securing his son's succession is not in the article; not repeated.

SKIPPED: article thin on the principalities themselves (most of it is Gorkha's campaigns against Nuwakot and Kathmandu) and it disagrees with the entry The entry says the kingdoms were ruled mostly by Thakuri dynasties; the article says Thakuri, Khas and Magar lineages. The entry has them conquered by Gorkha in the late eighteenth century; the article says annexation ran from 1744 to 1816.
The entry dates the Confucian temple and school to 1666; the article gives 1665. The text gives no year.

The article says King Sejong attempted to reunify the schools in 1407, before his reign began; the text gives only the 1424 absorption and no king's name. The entry's 1097 founding date is not in the article; not repeated. The order's own membership estimate and the 2015 patriarch were left out as present-day figures.
The article says Chiang Rai lies about 60 km to the south-west; the text gives the same distance from the other side.

The entry says he bought Bangalore from the Mughals in 1689; the article says he agreed with Venkoji in 1687 to buy it for Rs. 3 lakhs, the Mughals occupied it on 10 July 1687 and the payment went to Qasim Khan. The purchase is left out of the text. The article's opening story of battles with Sambhaji, venom arrows and leather suits is unsourced in tone and left out.

SKIPPED: article under 250 words of substance; the colony of Dorieus and the Macae are already in the description The entry says the colonists were driven out in its third year; the article says after about three years.

The article dates the Battle of Altimarlach to 1680 in one place and 1681 in another; the text gives no year for the battle. The article gives 1739 for the founding of the Grand Lodge of Scotland but also has James Sinclair resigning his office to the lodges on their foundation in 1736; no year given. The article says both that the clan supported the government in 1745 and that it was strongly Jacobite; the text follows its lead: sympathies Jacobite, chief for the government. The living chief is left out.
The article's sentence on a 'Hay–Sasha Treaty 1923' is garbled and was left out.
The article says the commission was also responsible for drafting the Constitution of Malaysia; left out as doubtful and not supported elsewhere in the article.

The article gives Erycius Puteanus the dates 1547–1646, which cannot fit a student of Lipsius; no dates given. The entry names the founder Jerome de Busleyden; the article Hieronymus van Busleyden, the same man.
The article lists Dominica (1632) under the company 'formerly as Compagnie de Saint-Christophe'; left out as before the company's founding.

The article states as fact that he was the first nobleman baptised by Patrick; the entry calls it later tradition, so the text frames it as tradition. The article gives both 'died c. 464' and a murder in 464; the text gives 464, which the entry's '5th century' allows.

Left out the article's claim that the Federated Malay States 'were not under the British colonial regime', which is doubtful and not needed. Scholarship funds and awards (1949 onwards) left out for length.
The article dates the battle of Mag Rath 'around 637'; the entry's d. 637 stands. The article gives 1907 for Ferguson's poem, which seems late (Ferguson died in 1886); the year is left out.

SKIPPED: article under 300 words, most of it already in the entry (Society of Suriname, peace of 1686, strict discipline, murder by mutineers in 1688) The article speaks only of peace with 'the Amerindian tribes' in 1686; the entry names the Kalina and Lokono.

The article names the 1914 arbitrator as the 'United States Attorney General' (the award is called the Fallo White, after Chief Justice Edward White); the text names no office. The article says the US demanded a ceasefire 'in late February', although fighting went on to 1 March; the date is left out.
The article gives the area as 791.9 km2 but also as 41,894 ha (about 419 km2), and its two province figures add up to neither; no area is given in the text.
The abolition in 1707 is not in the article and is not repeated.
The article states the move of the capital and the change of liturgical language as decisions 'according to the historians'; the entry calls them traditional; the text attributes them to historians.
The article lists the First Council in 561 but its section on it says 'the council of 563'; the entry has 561, and the text gives no year for it.

SKIPPED: article under 250 words of substance, and it contradicts itself on the date of his arrival The article has him arriving in Goryeo 'during the 1st month of 937, the 17th year of King Taejo's reign'; the 17th year of Taejo is 934, the entry's year. The article names a son, Tae Tosu, and the Hyeopgye and Yeongsun Tae and Miryang Dae clans as his descendants; too little for a longer text.

The article gives no year for the battles at Nimb and the Venna River (they precede the arrest of May 1751). The capture of Baroda and the Third Battle of Panipat, in the entry, are not in the article and are not repeated.

The article says the company was 'established in 1730' (the merger of 20 April 1730), with the royal licence and monopoly in 1732; the entry's dates begin with the charter of 1732. The text tells the 1730 merger as the origin and does not call it the founding. The dissolution in the 1840s is not in the article.

The article is about the Danteshwari Temple at Dantewada rather than the goddess; the text keeps to what it says of her worship. The meeting of the Shankhini and Dankini rivers, in the entry, is not in the article.

The article places the region 'east of the highlands in the east of the modern-day Central African Republic' and in south-western Sudan and north-western South Sudan; the entry says western South Sudan and the north-east of the Central African Republic. The text leaves the Central African Republic out. The Darb el-Arba'in, in the entry, is not in the article.

The article says he became associated with the Great God of Odessos 'during Roman rule of Dacia', which does not fit Odessos; the text gives no period for the identification. It dates the Metodievo relief to the '1st-3rd centuries BCE' while naming a Roman dedicant, Aelius Diogenes; no date is given. The entry's 'dish' is not in the article (it has altars).

SKIPPED: article of about 250 words, most of it a list of his children; the Tenbun war and the move to Yonezawa are already in the entry Article adds only: fifteenth head of the Date clan, childhood name Jiro, the character haru granted by Ashikaga Yoshiharu, the office of tendai of Mutsu, his wife Kubohime and their children (Date Terumune, Iwaki Chikataka, Rusu Masakage and others). It gives no years for the Tenbun war.

The article says Canabarro 'offered his services' to Rosas and also that Rosas sought the rebels' cooperation, then that Canabarro declared his loyalty; the text tells only the offer from Rosas and the reply. The Santa Catarina campaign with Garibaldi, in the entry, is not in the article.
The article does not give the year of the states' merger into Bombay; the entry's 1948 is not repeated.
The article gives the height of the Höfeler as 395 m in one place and calls it the Hofeler; the Bröhn at 405 m agrees with the entry. Calenberg, in the entry, is not in the article.
SKIPPED: article under 250 words of substance, much of it already in the description (founding, woodblocks, hand printing)

Left out the claim that Deshastha presence on the Desh dates to 1100-1700 BC and that they are the oldest Brahmin sub-caste: the article's reasoning is weak and self-promoting. The article names Bhaskara II, Dnyaneshwar and others as Deshasthas; not repeated.

The entry calls Airlangga his son-in-law; the article calls him his nephew and heir (son of his sister Mahendradatta). Neither relationship is stated in the text beyond his parents. The article states flatly that Srivijaya backed Haji Wurawari; the entry says probably. The text does not name Srivijaya's role in 1016.
SKIPPED: article under 250 words of substance; the one source is a brief remark in Caesar already given in the description
The article's opening says he 'was forced to run away to Britain' in August 1861, which appears to be garbled (the treaty ceded Lagos); left out.

The article says Duke Town (Akwa Akpa) was founded by Efik families who had left Creek Town, about 1650; the entry says it was founded with Creek Town and Old Town in the 17th century. Founding story left out. The article has King Archibong III crowned in 1878, which does not fit its own list of rulers; left out. Its religion section (the earth deity Ala, Ogbom) seems to describe the Igbo, not the Efik; left out.
SKIPPED: article under 250 words of substance: a few lines on the first performance and structure, critics quoted and a list of productions
The entry gives Constantín's reign as 789-820; the article gives fl. 793-820. No reign dates in the text.
The article says the Gorée building was built for the pirate slave traders Jean and Pierre Lafitte; left out as doubtful.

The article gives his death as 10 March 1939 in the lead but says his trial began on 19 March 1939 and that he was handed to the firing squad on the morning of the 19th; the text says only March 1939. Birth given as 1883 or 1884 (entry 1884); no birth year in the text.
The article places her husband's first expulsion in 1732; no year given in the text. The article gives no place of death.
Headings: 'Reign' used for his years as sultan.
The article says the Schellenberg family established the lordship in the 10th century; left out as doubtful (the castles are 1200 and 1250).
The article gives no Diodorus attribution; the text names no source. Dates kept as the entry's (no reign years given).

The article both calls the Ezhimala kingdom the predecessor of the Mushika dynasty and calls Nannan a member of the Mushika or Kolathiri family; the text keeps the two apart without deciding. The fifth-century date the article gives for Nannan's flight to Wayanad is left out (it sits oddly with the Sangam period). Rankings of the naval academy left out.

The article dates Bahram Khan's death to 737 AH (1336-1337), the entry has Fakhruddin seizing power on his master's death in 1338: the year is left out of the text. Sahidul Hasan dates the start of the reign to 734 AH (1333-1334) from coins; also left out.

The article has Fath-Ali Khan executed near Isfahan in July 1764; the entry dates his death to 1763. His death is therefore not told. The entry says he fought Mohammad Hasan Khan Qajar; the article says he joined the Qajars in 1757: the text says only that he joined them.
The article says the treaty was adopted on 9 September 1814 and came into force on 7 August 1815; the entry's 7 August 1815 swearing is consistent with this.

The article's lead gives his reign as 820-846 and his death as 847; the entry has king 820 to 847. The text gives no end year for the reign. Spelling Feidlimid kept as the entry's (the article heads it Fedelmid).

The entry says Fergus founded Soulseat and Whithorn Priory and revived the bishopric of Whithorn; the article says it is uncertain who revived the diocese (c. 1128) and that there is no proof Fergus did, and it does not name Soulseat or Whithorn Priory. The revival is left out of the text. The entry speaks of a failed revolt against Malcolm IV; the article says the reasons for the invasion are unknown: the text gives no reason.

The article calls Fézensac an 8th-century Carolingian creation (counts Burgund, Liutard c. 801, Arnold in 864); the entry says it was created in the 10th century for a son of the dukes of Gascony. The Carolingian counts are left out of the text and the 926 grant is told.

The entry dates the inaugurations and councils to the 14th and 15th centuries; the article makes the islands the administrative centre from the 13th to the 15th century. The text gives no starting century for the lordship's use of the site.
The article names Scott both Major Hugh Scott and Colonel Hugh L. Scott; the text gives no rank. American casualty figures differ by source (15-21 killed); the text attributes them.

The article says the site was designated a World Heritage Site; left out as doubtful. The 1740 fort is said to have been destroyed in the Spanish counterattack; the text does not say who damaged it, matching the entry's wording.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance and adds little beyond the description (the 46 BCE boundary of Africa Vetus and Nova and a Pliny quotation)
The article does not mention the municipal status of 1872-1887 or the extension of citizenship in 1946 that the entry gives; it dates the first grant of citizenship rights to 1848.

The article contradicts itself on the deposition: it says he was declared forfeit and expelled in 1706 and also that he was deposed in 1708 (the entry's year, with Joseph I); it also says 'his rule began in 1706'. The text gives no year for the forfeiture and keeps 1708 only for the confiscation.
The article says Dupetit Thouars 'formally annexed the islands' in November 1843 while also saying the protectorate continued; the text says only that he deposed the queen.

The article gives his death as 11 June 1843 in the lead and 21 June 1843 later: only the year is given. It dates his appointment to Martinique to 1817 in the lead and his governorship to 1818-1826 later: no start year is given.

The entry says the Zwiefalten frescoes were painted from 1751; the article's list gives 1728-1729 and 1747-1753. No dates are given for Zwiefalten in the text. The article lists a Weingarten altar painting dated 1783, after his death; left out.

The article does not mention Riel's surrender (in the entry). It calls Bremner a Scotch-Indian; the entry a Métis trader: the text gives no label for him. His death (25 January 1898) is not told, so the heading is Legacy.
The article says she was at first an Arian Christian who turned to Nicene Christianity; the entry says she learned of Christianity from a traveller. Her earlier faith is left out of the text.

The entry says the radical faction fought on until agreements of 2000 and 2001; the article mentions only the radicals' 2001 peace agreement, so no year of a settlement is given in the text. The article also reports that FRUD-C attacks continued after 2001 (100 deaths up to 2014, a policeman killed in 2021, the Garabtisan barracks attack of 2022). The text mentions the 2021 and 2022 attacks as made under the FRUD-C name without saying the faction as a whole kept fighting, so as not to contradict the entry.

The article says Fu received the dukedom of Ying after the Yunnan campaign; the entry agrees. It also notes historians thought the lack of a dukedom after Sichuan an inadequate reward (left out for length).
The article gives the date of death as 10 August 1128, consistent with the entry's year.

The article calls the southern kingdom Dali throughout (Nanzhao only in its lead); the text uses Dali for the later border fighting and avoids naming the 866 enemy, which the entry calls Nanzhao. The article names the new circuit Jinghai; the entry gives Tinh Hai (Jinghai), so it is not repeated.
The article dates construction to between 70 and 80; the entry says probably the 70s or 80s, so no construction range is printed, only Agricola's campaign around 80 and the coins of 86.

The article lists Looking for Dilmun under 1961 (with an ISBN/date warning); the entry gives 1969, so the text names no year for it. The article names the University of Aarhus, not the Moesgaard Museum named in the entry; the text says only University of Aarhus. The article says 'Hellenic period'; the text writes Hellenistic age. The Barbar temple of the entry is not in the article; the Saar temple is.
The article does not mention the Siraya by name or the romanised Siraya writing named in the entry; nothing is added on them.

The entry dates the taking of Évora to 1165. The article gives September 1164 as most likely, notes Ibn Sahib's 1165 (thought a year off) and the Cronica dos Godos' 1166. The text gives no dates for the conquests of 1164-1167. The entry says he went on to capture Trujillo and Caceres after Evora; the article's order (Ibn Sahib and the later dating) puts Trujillo before Evora. The text lists the places without an order.

The article counts five Naval Laws (1898, 1900, 1906, 1908, 1912); the entry speaks of acts of 1898 and 1900. The text calls the later three amendments, as the article's own table does. The article is inconsistent on the First Law: 16 battleships in three years, seven battleships, ships to be built by 1904, total to be attained by 1903. The text gives only 19 battleships with seven new. On the Second Law it gives 1901-1917 in the text and 'by 1920' in the table: no completion year printed. The article gives the First Law as passed 26 March 1898 and signed 10 April 1898.

The entry gives his Lagos governorship as 1891-1897; the article says he was transferred to the Bahamas in 1898. The text gives no year for the end of his time in Lagos. The article's lead says he was Administrator of the Gambia and dealt with 'the native king'; the body names Fode Kaba and Musa Molo, used here.

The article says her father died when she was 11, but its family list gives him the dates 1705-1758 (she was born in 1739); the text gives no age for her orphaning. Her father's name is given as Kim Eun-gyeol in the biography and Kim Eung-ryeol in the family list; the text uses the second, which carries dates.
The article calls him Count Giuseppe Prina without saying when or by whom he was ennobled; left out.

SKIPPED: The article says nothing of Gopakapattana or the Kadambas; its history section is about Old Goa (Velha Goa), the Portuguese capital, which it partly confuses with this place, and the rest is census figures and geography (it even places the village near the Mandovi). Too little of substance on the entry's subject.

The article states plainly that the mosque was built in the 15th century during Korau's reign (1445-1495); the entry calls the date traditional (late 15th or early 16th century). The text ties it to Almaghili's visit late in the 15th century and gives no reign dates for Korau. The article places the lookout use in its Mythology section; the text attributes it to tradition. The article does not say the tower is of mud brick.

The entry dates the office to 1532, when it was abolished with the Signoria. The article says it survived until the Medici abolished the republican constitution on their return in 1530, and also that 1512 marked the end of the republican system. The text gives no year for its end. The article's wording on Soderini's fall is muddled ('Piero decided to abandon the city'); the text says only that he lost office at the end of 1512 when the Medici returned.

The article gives two different sizes for the largest shaft grave (6.5 x 4.1 m in the lead, 4.50 x 6.40 m under Finds); no size is printed. The article places the circle both south and southeast of the Lion Gate; not repeated.

The entry says Congress broke the remaining land into six smaller reservations in 1889; the article speaks of five and lists five. The text names five 'among them' and gives no number. The entry describes the reservation as present-day South Dakota west of the Missouri; the article adds land in Nebraska. Not repeated.

The article contradicts itself on the militia's end: it 'disbanded more than a year before' 1777 in the lead, but 'faded away after' 1791 in the History section. The text gives no date for its end. The ranger regiment's disbandment is given as 1779 in the lead only; left out.
The article dates the poem to the seventh century BC, as the entry does.

SKIPPED: The article has under 200 words of substance and adds little beyond the entry (it also differs on the revolt, giving 1497 and a night attack that captured him, then his release); too thin for a longer text.
The article says he died at Aigues-Mortes 'sometime in 1273'; the entry dates his death to 1274. The year is left out of the text.
The article spells the Aztec ruler Ahuizotl; the entry writes Ahuitzotl, so he is not named in the text. The article gives no date for the siege; the entry's 'late 1490s' is not repeated.
The article calls it a five-day uprising; the entry says the rebels were defeated 'within weeks'. The duration is left out of the text.

The article gives his birth as 1723; the entry has c. 1708. The article dates his regency from 1749; the entry says after 1748. Both points are left out of the text. The article's section on 1748 (Subedar of Sirhind against Ahmad Shah Durrani) is confused and was not used.

The entry calls Hajo the seat of the Koch Hajo kingdom from 1581; the article does not say this, naming Koch Hajo only as a Koch chief of the early 16th century. The kingdom is not mentioned in the text. The article's Politics and Notable people sections (current MLA) were left out.
The article's lead gives his birth as 10 April 1910, but its Early life section says he was born between 1910 and 1915; the birth year is left out of the text.

The article dates his exile 1922 to 1931 and says he was allowed back in January 1931; the entry says he was exiled until 1930. The date of his return is left out of the text. The article's lead names his birthplace as Mìtahato village, its Education section as Kambūi; only Kiambu district is given.

The entry says the Türkmen-Karahöyük inscription was found in 2019; the article says a farmer found the stele in 2018 and told the researchers in the summer of 2019. The year of the find is left out of the text.

The article's lead says the last group disbanded in 1890; its Aftermath says the Haw continued their depredations until the mid-1890s. The end date is left out of the text. The entry's sack of Luang Prabang in 1887 is not in the article.
The article gives his birth as c. 1410; the entry has c. 1400. The birth year is left out of the text. The article is general and thinly sourced; the text keeps to what it states.
The article gives his birth as 28 March 1692; the entry has c. 1691. The birth year is left out of the text. The article reports, and doubts, a journey to England around 1740; left out.

The entry says Carloff obtained land from Fante rulers and founded Fort Carolusborg at Cape Coast in 1653. The article says his land contracts were with the chief of the Efutu, and that his successor Isaac Melville started building Fort Carolusborg in 1653 while Carloff was in Europe. Neither the land grant nor the fort's founding is told in the text.
The article is short; the text uses nearly all of it.
SKIPPED: Article under 300 words; beyond the entry it adds only a few lines (Hili 8, fingerprints at Hili II, the 2011 inscription), too little for a longer text.
The entry says the movement was crushed near Jinja in late 1987; the article does not mention Jinja but ends with Alice's arrest in Kenya on 26 December 1987. No conflict in the text.
The article is short; the text uses most of it.
The article says 'some 3–40%' of Huang's soldiers died of illness in Lingnan, an apparent slip; no figure is given in the text.

The article gives his death as 26 November 1508 in the castle of Xàtiva; the entry dates him d. 1503, which is the year of his capture at Naples. Death year left out. The entry has Ferdinand II defeating him in 1487; the article says he held the county until 1487 and fled in 1488. The year of his flight is left out. The article says his wife resisted 'heroically'; the word is dropped.

The article gives the occupation of Hunza as 22 December and the taking of Baltit Fort as 23 December, and in one place has both rulers fleeing to Chinese Turkestan while elsewhere the Mir of Nagar is arrested in his city. These details are left vague or follow the Aftermath section. The article's 'Failed attempt to take Chalt fort' section is set in spring 1891 and is confused; left out.
The article does not say how the Wendat text survived or was recovered; nothing on that was added.

The article dates his brother Suleiman's death to late 1124 or late 1130; left out. The article also says he made an attack on the crusaders 'at Jerusalem' in 1152 and was defeated; left out as unclear.

The article puts the gap before Humban-tahrah at 350 years after the last two Middle Elamite kings; the entry says Elam disappears from the record for about three centuries after his reign. The length of the gap is left out. The article gives his reign as c. 1120–1100 BCE and gives no date for the battle at the Ulai; the entry's c. 1110 BCE is not contradicted.

The article gives the atoll's total area both as 3,152 km2 and as approximately 2,900 km2; total area left out, only the dry land (38.5 km2) given. The article says the republic 'survived until September 1963' and also that it 'collapsed' after Thinadhoo was destroyed in 1962; the end date is left out.
The article does not name his father; the entry's Ammishtamru II is not contradicted. The final paragraph attributes the article's own interpretation to historians.

The article dates him fl. c. 1950 BC; the entry has r. c. 2000 BCE at the end of the Ur III period. The article's date is left out; the link with Ishbi-Erra is kept. Short article; about 270 words written.
The entry mentions the ruling party's youth wing as perpetrators; the excerpt does not, and says nothing against it. Death toll estimates are already in the entry and not repeated.
SKIPPED: article too thin: about 150 words on her, most already in the entry; the rest is about naditu priestesses of the same name
SKIPPED: article too thin: its substance is already in the entry, apart from one quoted 1874 gazette notice
The Museum of Inuit Art in Toronto (2007-2016) and the Inuit Art Society are left out.
The article does not name the Caristii; the entry's statement is not contradicted. The 2025 re-examination of graffiti from Las Ermitas at Espejo is left out.

The article spells the names in Bidar inconsistently (Kasim-Barid, Kasmim Barid, Amir Birad) and the general as Asad Kahan, Ashad Khan and Asad Khan; the Bidar ruler of the second campaign is left unnamed. The article gives no year for his accession; the entry's 1510 is not contradicted.

The article gives his death as 3 November 1918 in the lead and 2 November in the text; the entry says he was killed in prison on 1 November 1918. The date is left out. Born 4 December 1884 per the article; not printed, as the entry's dates cover it.
The article says he was mayor from 1919 to 1929 (elected 1919); the entry says 1918 to 1929. The year of his first election is left out.
SKIPPED: article too thin: about 270 words, most of it already in the entry
The 2016 cover by Mani Kollengode is left out.
The article's Character section (deep religious feeling, great nobility) is the older biography's praise; only Clarendon's attributed judgement is kept.

The article says Wright himself regained control of Savannah on 29 December 1778; the entry says he returned in 1779 after British forces reoccupied the town. The date is left out and the wording follows the entry. The article says his wife Sarah died in 1774 and, in the family section, that Sarah Maidman died in 1763; her death is left out.

The article's estimate of 1,000 to 1,500 residents matches the entry; the 8,000 figure is given as the Shamu-koku fūdo gunki's own estimate. Left out the Grand Palace weapon museum display and the travel agency guide (present-day detail).
The article says he returned to Saint-Tropez in 1835 and also that he went to France on leave in June 1834, returning 18 months later; the text gives June 1834 and the 18 months only.
The article gives 538 as the year the temple was built; the entry ties it to the move of 538, which agrees.
Left out the article's mention of a descendant who is a present-day television reporter and the daughter on the 1972 banknote (living people).

Dates: the article gives c. 770–850 and calls him an 8th-century and 8/9th-century scholar; the entry says 9th century. No dates given in the text. The entry says Gunabhadra finished the Adipurana; the article says Gunabhadra completed the Uttarapurana and co-authored parts of the Mahapurana. The text says only that Gunabhadra worked on the Mahapurana. The article contradicts itself on the Harivamsa Purana (lead: by an earlier Jinasena of the Punnata Sangh; section: sometimes attributed to this Jinasena or Gunabhadra). Left out.
Short article (about 300 words); three sections at the low end of the length.

The article says Printz returned to Sweden in 1654; the entry says he left the colony in 1653. The year of his departure is left out. The article calls him the third governor of New Sweden; the entry does not number him.
The entry says he was shot dead; the article says only that he was killed. The text says killed.

The article gives the fall of Fort Christina as 15 August 1655; the text gives only the year. The article says he was appointed assistant councillor under Governor Printz, which sits oddly with the entry's governorship of 1654-1655; left out.

The article gives the Twi dictionary's publication as 1881 in one place and 1871 (with an update in 1881) in another; the text gives 1881 only, for the two-volume dictionary named in the main narrative. The article says he applied to the seminary in May 1847 and started in September 1848; the text says he entered in 1848.

The article gives 1834 for his return to Europe and 1833 for the Afghan botanical journey; the text keeps the 1833 journey and gives no year for the return. The article spells Claude Auguste Court here; the Allard article has Claude August Court.
The article names Klemens Wenzel Lothar von Metternich; shortened in the text.
The entry dates his death c. 1649; the article says after 1649. The text gives only the last record of him in 1649. Aruba and Bonaire (in the entry) are not in the article.

Birth: the article gives 1588 (Lethbridge) and says the NEHGS concludes he was probably born no later than 1600; the entry gives c. 1601. No birth year in the text. The article records his death as 15 March 1664/5 (Old Style); the text gives 1665, as the entry does.
Left out the article's present-day description of the university's size.

The entry says Aceh attacked the town; the article says Aceh sacked Kota Batu, near Johor Lama, in 1564, before the capital was set up at Johor Lama in the early 1570s. The text follows the article without contradicting the entry.

The article contradicts itself on the peace process: the lead speaks of a truce in March 1991 and a 1992 Kourou peace accord; the body has a June 1989 ceasefire and an Accord of Kourou signed on 21 July (1989).
